Korean letters are grouped into **syllable blocks**. A block always starts with a consonant. If a syllable starts with a vowel sound, we write the silent consonant `ㅇ` in front: ㅇ + ㅏ = **아** [a].
Vertical vowels stand to the **right** of ㅇ, horizontal ones go **under** it.

**애** (ㅏ+ㅣ) and **에** (ㅓ+ㅣ) are both pronounced like “e” in “bed”. Modern Seoul speakers don't distinguish them — you just learn the spelling of each word. Same for **얘 / 예** (ye).

Put a consonant in the place of ㅇ: ㄱ + ㅏ = **가**, ㄴ + ㅗ = **노**.

ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅈ sound almost like k, t, p, ch at the beginning of a word, and like g, d, b, j between vowels: **고기** [ko-gi], **바다** [pa-da].
Korean has three kinds of k, t, p, ch: **plain** (가), **aspirated** with a puff of air (카) and **tense** — tight throat, no air (까).
Hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth: on **카 타 파 차** it should move, on **까 따 빠 짜** it should stay still.

At the start of a word 의 is “ui”: **의자** [ui-ja]. After a consonant it sounds like ㅣ: 희 [hi].
받침: the consonant at the bottom
A consonant can sit at the bottom of a block: ㅂ + ㅏ + ㅂ = **밥**. This final consonant is called **받침**.
Many letters, but at the end of a syllable they reduce to seven sounds. The final sound is short and “unreleased”.
ㅇ at the bottom is not silent
At the top ㅇ is silent, at the bottom it is “ng”: **방** [pang].
밤 / 밥 / 방 / 반 differ only in the final sound — great listening practice!
